1:
The chapter lifts into a new and loftier strain, and the witnesses feel at once that they have passed out of Job's complaint into a set piece of surpassing grandeur. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott names its design: here Job draws out a magnificent contrast between human skill and ingenuity on the one hand and Divine wisdom on the other, and the whole difficulty for the ordinary reader, he warns, lies in not perceiving that the person spoken of throughout is man and not God — man who possesses and exercises this mastery over nature, yet remains ignorant of wisdom unless God bestow it upon him. That Job should say so, Ellicott adds, is but natural after his painful experience of the want of wisdom in his friends. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke opens with unfeigned admiration, calling the chapter the oldest and finest piece of natural history in the world; and he fixes the first term philologically, for the word rendered “vein” (motsa) signifies literally a going out, a mine or place dug in the earth whence the silver ore is extracted, the ore lying in veins or loads that run in certain directions, so that the closing clause is better read “a place for gold which they refine.”

The reformed John Gill asks why silver is named before the costlier gold, and answers that it is not for its worth, since gold is preferable to it as brass is to iron, but because silver was likely first known and first in use, especially in the coinage of money — for Scripture speaks of shekels of silver in Abraham's day before ever a golden coin is mentioned. The very name of silver, he observes, comes from a word signifying “desire,” because it is desirable to men, answering to so many uses that the craving after it grows criminal and becomes the root of all evil; and now there is a “vein” for it in the earth, running as veins run in a man's body, in ramifications like the branches of trees.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley sets the hymn in the flow of the argument: having discoursed of God's providences toward the wicked, Job here declares that the ground of those providences is one of the depths of Divine wisdom, not discoverable by any mortal; men have indeed a wisdom whereby they search out hidden things, the veins of silver and gold, but this is a wisdom of a higher nature and out of man's reach. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the lesson that will govern the whole: what a great way the wit of man may go in diving into the depths of nature and seizing its riches; yet does it follow that men may by their wit comprehend why some wicked prosper and others are punished? By no means. The caverns of the earth may be discovered, but not the counsels of heaven; and the refrain the hymn is building toward, at v.12, already hangs unspoken over the glittering inventory of the mine.
2:
The catalogue of metals goes on, and the witnesses follow it down from the precious to the serviceable: “iron is taken out of the earth, and brass is molten out of the stone.” The reformed John Gill marks the contrast with the silver of the opening line, for iron is had easily and in great plenty, being more common, lying nearer the surface, and said here to be taken “out of the dust”; melted in the furnace it yields a metal so serviceable that scarce anything can be done without it, and therefore, with brass, of the earliest invention. He recalls the primitive craft behind the verse, naming Tubalcain the son of Lamech, whom the heathen made their Vulcan, the instructor of every artificer in brass and iron.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the line “iron is taken out of the dust, and he poureth forth stone as copper,” and observe that it is worthy of remark that the last-named metal, with which the whole description is then closely connected, is copper. They set the verse at the head of the mining strophe, whose several stages — the shaft broken away from those who tarry above, the swinging far from men — the following verses will unfold; and they note that among the expositors of these strophes are two men actually acquainted with mining, a director and an inspector of mines, whose technical observations they weigh, one referring the descent to a cross-bar attached to a rope, another the letting-off of the water to its earliest mode.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke attends to the second clause and its chemistry. Iron, he says, is hidden under the earth, and men have found out the method of separating it from its ore; and “brass is molten out of the stone” must mean copper, for brass is a factitious metal and the Hebrew nechushah properly denotes copper — literally, the stone is poured out for brass. Yet, Clarke allows, if the common rendering be retained, the process of brass-making may itself be intended, for that metal is formed from copper melted with the stone calamine, so that the stone is in that sense poured out to make brass. The witnesses do not divide over the sense; together they let the verse do its quiet work, ranging the useful metals beside the costly ones so that, when the great question breaks in, the whole wealth of the earth — gold and silver, iron and copper alike — may be set on one side of the scale and found wanting against the wisdom that is weighed on the other.
3:
The description now follows the miner underground, and the witnesses read the verse as a portrait of human daring: “he setteth an end to darkness, and searcheth out all perfection: the stones of darkness, and the shadow of death.” The reformed John Gill notes that some understand the whole of God, who by making the luminaries fixed the periods of light and darkness, or who determined the appointed times when the hidden things of nature should be brought to light; but he judges it rather to be spoken of the miner, who, opening his mine and carrying his lamp into it, puts an end to the darkness that had reigned there, unbroken, from the creation. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott turns the sentence firmly in the same direction, reading it “man setteth an end to darkness, and searcheth out to the furthest bound the stones of darkness and the shadow of death” — for it is man's mastery, not God's, that the hymn is here recounting.

Keil and Delitzsch, the other grammatical-historical voice, describe the operation more minutely and settle a difficult word: nachal, which elsewhere means a valley or the bed of a river, here signifies the excavation made in the earth, and, as what follows shows, one in a perpendicular direction — therefore the shaft. They record the debate of the mining men over the term, one contending for “valley” in the sense of a worked surface-vein, in which a small shaft is sunk and the ore wrought from both sides at once. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps to the same subject, taking the words to point out the persevering industry of man in penetrating the bowels of the earth after metals and precious stones; even the stones that lay hidden he has digged for and brought to light, and has gone in directions where the solar light could never be transmitted, so that he appears to have travelled into the very regions of the shadow of death, as Mr. Good renders it, delving into the region of darkness to examine, to its uttermost limit, the stones of darkness and death-shade.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley gives the two hard phrases their compact gloss: “perfection” is whatever is deeply wrought in the deepest caverns, and “stones of darkness” are the precious stones that lie hid in the dark bowels of the earth, where no living thing can dwell. The witnesses do not finally divide over the reference; though Gill records the older reading that made God the subject, the weight of them all falls on man the miner, whose lamp ends the ancient night of the mine and whose hand rifles the very shadow of death — and it is precisely this triumph, pressed to its furthest bound, that the coming refrain will show to fall short of wisdom.
4:
The verse is one of the acknowledged cruxes of the chapter, and the witnesses handle it with open caution: “the flood breaketh out from the inhabitant; even the waters forgotten of the foot: they are dried up, they are gone away from men.” The reformed John Gill takes it of the peril that dogs the mine, reading “so that there is no inhabitant” of it — for the miner may be called its inhabitant, who lives there continually, and when a flood of water arises, as usually happens in mines, he is forced to flee and make haste to save his life.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke owns the passage “very difficult,” and lays out the two roads interpreters have taken. If it refer to mining, it points to the waters that spring up when the miners have sunk to a considerable depth, so that the mine is drowned and abandoned, forgotten of the foot, no man treading there any more; the waters rise to a level with the spring and are then carried away from men, the stream lost in the bowels of the earth. But he records also the conjecture of Mr. Peters that the verse, like a place in an earlier chapter, glances rather at navigation, then in its infancy — nachal being a torrent or arm of the sea that divides nations and interrupts their commerce until the help of ships be found; on which reading the men “forgotten of the foot” cannot walk over the waters but must embark, and dwindle from sight as they depart the land, and are tossed to and fro by the waves, an image Clarke likens to the psalmist's ship reeling like a drunken man in Ps. 107:26-27. For all that, Clarke cannot doubt the passage applies solely to mining, and adopts the first sense, adding Coverdale's older turn about the river that parts asunder the strange, unmannerly people.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott is equally frank that the words are “very uncertain,” and offers two renderings of his own: either “man breaketh open a shaft where none sojourneth,” so that the labourers, forgotten where none passeth by, hang afar from the haunts of men and flit to and fro; or else the flood breaking out from its inhabitants, the very course of rivers being subject to the will of man, who so obliterates their marks that those who walk over the place forget it was ever a river. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley keeps to the mine: while men are searching, the water breaks in upon them out of that part of the earth the miners inhabit, in places untrodden by the foot of man, and is then dried up, or drawn up by engines made for the purpose, that the work be not hindered. The witnesses divide, then, less against one another than against the obscurity of the Hebrew itself, most of them following the miner into his flooded shaft while one reported voice hears in the words the earliest venture of the ship.
5:
From the depths the verse lifts its eye a moment to the surface and then plunges again: “as for the earth, out of it cometh bread: and under it is turned up as it were fire.” The reformed John Gill takes the bread simply for bread-corn, the wheat that, cast into the earth, rises and brings forth fruit and, ground to flour, makes fine bread; and he garnishes the note with the old traveller's lore of the West Indians who made their bread of a root they called jucca, and of Caesar's soldiers who in their distress made bread of a root steeped in milk. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix the grammar against the misreadings, insisting that “the earth” here denotes not the interior but the surface — whose proper name, adamah, they trace to a root meaning a flat covering — set in deliberate opposition to “that which is beneath,” so that the one line looks to the corn above and the other to the fire below.

What that fire may be is the point over which the witnesses genuinely part. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke thinks it a combustible fossil, some stone-coal such as was dug up in parts of Arabia; but he records too the Chaldee's ancient fancy of a central fire, the place called hell, and the Vulgate's reading that the land was destroyed by fire, in which he detects a probable allusion to the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah, and even carries that catastrophe into the next verses, where no path is left and the whole region lies under the dead lake. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley keeps two possibilities open: the fire is coals, brimstone, and other materials of fire — unless, as some suppose, it refer to a central fire. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads it wholly of the mine and the mountain: while the ploughman and reaper till the surface, the miner far below maintains perpetual fires, as does the volcanic mountain, luxuriant and fertile on its sides. So the debate is real and unresolved — whether the fire beneath the corn-bearing crust is the miner's kindled coal, the brimstone of a buried judgment, or the deep central heat of the earth itself. The witnesses do not settle it; they leave the verse charged with its double wonder, that the same ground which yields the gentle bread of men hides beneath it a furnace, so that the hymn's picture of the earth is at once a granary and a hearth of fire.
6:
The inventory of the mine reaches its richest line: “the stones of it are the place of sapphires: and it hath dust of gold.” The reformed John Gill takes the sapphire as put for all precious stones — a most excellent gem of a sky colour flecked with golden specks, one of the stones set in the high priest's breastplate — and, after his manner, hears in its blue the pavement under the feet of the God of Israel and the beauty of the church in her latter glory. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps to the mineralogy, calling “the place of sapphires” the gangue or matrix, the very bed in which the stone is found, and reading the second clause plainly as gold dust.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch weigh the harder question, whether “it hath dust of gold” belongs to the sapphire or stands on its own. They allow that the ancients — Theophrastus, who calls the sapphire as it were sprinkled with gold, and Pliny, who speaks of the golden points that glitter in it — might warrant referring the dust to the stone; but they observe that this holds not of the true sapphire at all but of the azure stone, the lapis lazuli so often confounded with it, whose most prized variety is shot through with glittering points of iron pyrites. On the whole, with Schultens and Schlottmann, they judge such a collateral remark about gold-dusted sapphire awkward and unlikely, and take the clause rather as a clean and suitable appellation of gold ore, the earth that in itself is black yet holds the shining metal. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley likewise makes the sapphire the most eminent of stones, put for all the rest, mixed among the common rock and cut and polished from it, and takes the “dust” for a second and distinct kind of gold, the fine dust as against the metal found in the mass. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott simply lets the wonder stand: so ingenious is man that he discovers a place whose very stones are sapphires and whose dust is gold, and a path besides that no bird of prey has known. Beneath their small differences the witnesses agree — the verse heaps the costliest things of earth into a single clause precisely so that the hymn may, in a moment, sweep them all aside; the rock that is a bed of sapphire and a mine of gold is still no bed and no mine for wisdom.
7:
The hymn now measures the miner's reach against the keenest eyes in creation: “there is a path which no fowl knoweth, and which the vulture's eye hath not seen.” The reformed John Gill reads the path as the track the miners drive to the ores and the beds of precious stones, a way never seen and never to be discovered by the sharpest-sighted of birds. He fixes on the eagle in particular, the king of birds and the swiftest, whose very Greek name he thinks derived from the Hebrew word here; eager and quick-sighted as it is, marking its prey at a great distance and in its most secret lurking-place, yet it could never look into the bowels of the earth, and in this it is outdone by the diligent and laborious miner, who is at no loss to make his way into the darkest recesses of the ground.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke lingers over the marvel of bird-instinct — how the fowls traverse vast forests and return in all weathers without missing their track, and the birds of passage cross kingdoms and oceans without deviating in the least — and yet, he says, in this one thing even the keen scent of the vulture and the piercing sight of the eagle would be of no use, for the way into the hidden mines lies utterly beyond them. He turns the verse, characteristically, into a rebuke of the confident geologists of his own day, who talk of the structure of the globe as if they had examined it from the centre to the circumference, though no man has pierced two miles into the earth; all such things, he says, are to them a path no fowl knoweth, and they lack the simple heart to seek the wisdom that might be found. And he records the strange turn one of the Chaldee Targums gives the verse, making the path the way of the tree of life, which even Satan, flying like a bird, has not known, nor the eye of Eve beheld, nor the serpent found. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley keeps the plain sense, taking the path for one in the bowels of the earth and the vulture's eye for that very quick and strong sight which searches all places for its prey. The witnesses agree in the wonder: the buried road that the miner treads is closed to the sharpest eye that hunts above it, and man alone, of all the creatures, has found the way down.
8:
The parallel of the birds is matched at once by a parallel of the beasts: “the lion's whelps have not trodden it, nor the fierce lion passed by it.” The reformed John Gill dwells on the ranging violence of such creatures, exceeding fierce and voracious, eager after their prey, that search every hole and corner and rove through the dens and caves of the earth; and yet, he says, even these never traversed the ways the miners cut to fetch out the wealth of the ground. After his wont he lifts the image into a spiritual key, for wicked men are sometimes likened to lions for their cruelty and oppression, and tyrannical princes and persecutors above all — the kings of Assyria and Babylon, and Nero the Roman — yet these never trod the way of holiness, nor knew the wisdom of God in a mystery, nor the Lord of life; and he notes that the former clause may as well be rendered “the children of pride,” the proud beasts that own no master.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws out the point the pairing is made for: the lion ranges all places for its prey, and the birds and beasts have often led men to places they would otherwise never have found, guiding the hunter by their tracks and haunts; but they could not lead men to these mines, and the finding out of them is a special gift of God. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, surveying the whole passage together, sets the same picture in its frame, that the miner treads the path no fowl knoweth, unseen by the vulture's quick and piercing eye, and untrodden by the lion's whelps that traverse all the paths of the wilderness. The witnesses do not divide; together they complete the great comparison the two verses make. The strongest and the swiftest of the wild creatures, the fiercest hunters of the upper world, for all their ranging have never found the buried road; man alone descends it. And that, in the movement of the hymn, is the very height of the human triumph the poet has been building — a triumph raised so high on purpose, that the question about to break in may fall from a greater height and land with more weight: man has outrun the eagle and the lion into the dark, and still he has not found where wisdom dwells. The poet lets that irony stand as the very peak from which the following verses will look down, and from which the great refrain will ask its unanswerable question of a creature who has mastered everything under the earth except the one thing worth the mastering.
9:
The miner now sets his hand to the living rock: “he putteth forth his hand upon the rock; he overturneth the mountains by the roots.” The reformed John Gill keeps the discourse fixed on the digger in the earth, who, meeting a rock or a ridge of flint, is not discouraged but goes to work upon it, laying his hammer against it and beating it to pieces, cutting through it with proper instruments, and, as Pliny observed, using fire and vinegar to make his way — and so, splitting the stubborn stone, oftentimes lays bare the gold or silver or precious stones hidden within it. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the same industry, man putting his hand upon the rock and breaking it to extract the metals it contains, and “overturning the mountains” by excavating and undermining and digging them away in search of what they hold — not poetically only, he insists, but literally the case in many instances. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds the finer craft the words imply, the process of tunnelling and excavating and of cutting canals and lining them with stone, in the course of which many precious things are discovered; and he marvels that the ancient canals and cisterns were made so accurately that they held their water and did not so much as weep or trickle.

Yet here the witnesses genuinely part over whose hand it is. Where Gill, Clarke, and Ellicott read the whole of the human miner, the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley refers this verse and the two that follow to God himself, taking them to name other eminent works of the Almighty, who overturns the rocks and produces new rivers. So a real division runs beneath the line, the same crux Ellicott had flagged at the head of the chapter: are the mighty acts of these verses — the hand upon the rock, the rivers cut among the stones, the floods bound from overflowing — the achievements of man in his mining, or the works of God in his providence? The three read them of man, and Wesley of God. The difference, for all that, does not break the movement of the hymn, for on either reading the verses heap up power upon power, whether of the creature or the Creator, only to make the coming refrain the more startling; if it be man, his mightiest labour cannot buy wisdom, and if it be God, then the wisdom man seeks is hid in the very hand that overturns the mountains.
10:
The great labour goes on among the rocks: “he cutteth out rivers among the rocks; and his eye seeth every precious thing.” The reformed John Gill reads it of the miner who cleaves the rocks asunder to find the value hidden in their clefts, or who, cutting his way through them, opens a course for the rivers and floods of water to drain off from his workings, so that he may go on with more comfort and success — though sometimes, he notes, the shafts are sunk so far below the base of the rock, forty or fifty fathom deep, that the water at last defeats them. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke describes the same engineering in the terms of his own day: the miner cuts canals and adits in the rock and drives levels far underground, continued a great way and fitly compared to rivers or channels; he sinks his shafts and drives his levels precisely that his eye may light on where the precious minerals lie, of which he is in eager pursuit.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch work at a nicety of the Hebrew, the phrase rendered “rivers among the rocks.” They reject the reading that would make the miner gather the trickling drippings of the watercourses into channels for use, urging that the verb here will not directly signify to collect; yet they allow that its proper sense of restraining or coercing lies close at hand, as is plain from the kindred Arabic words for a dam and a reservoir, so that the notion of binding and catching the water is not far off — a sense they will carry into the binding of the floods in the next verse. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley adds only the smallest and aptest gloss on the second clause, that the miner's eye sees even those precious things which no human art or industry was ever able to discover. The witnesses do not divide over the picture; they let it stand as the near summit of the whole account, the miner not merely descending into the dark but mastering the very waters of the deep, turning rivers out of their beds and threading the rock with channels, until nothing precious can hide from his searching eye — nothing, that is, save the one thing the hymn is about to ask for. The more the miner uncovers, the witnesses imply, the plainer it grows that his very success only measures the distance he still stands from wisdom; he has bared every hidden thing but the one that matters, and the deeper he drives the nearer he comes to the question his skill can never answer.
11:
The mining panel closes on its highest note of mastery: “he bindeth the floods from overflowing; and the thing that is hid bringeth he forth to light.” The reformed John Gill dwells on the vividness of the Hebrew in the first clause, which he renders “he bindeth the floods from weeping”: as the miner cuts through rock to drain his works, so he uses other means to keep the waters back from breaking in, binding them so firmly and stopping every avenue so close that they cannot so much as ooze, or distil and drop like a tear from the eye. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the same triumph over the water, the miner preventing the springs from drowning the mine and turning rivers from their wonted course to bring to light what lay hidden under their beds — a work, he says, both difficult and costly, done in his own age by the steam-engine, though how the ancients managed it he cannot tell, save that they dug deep after the riches of the earth. He crowns the note with Pliny's stern sentence, that we descend into the bowels of the earth and seek for wealth even in the abodes of departed spirits, and with Ovid's lament over the iron age, when greedy mortals rummaged the earth's store and dug out the precious ore that the prudent gods had hidden next to hell, so that cursed steel and more accursed gold gave mischief birth.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the whole passage to a close and a moral. Man must grapple with the subterraneous waters, binding the floods from overflowing at the peril of his life, and then at last he makes something of his toil: that which was hidden he brings forth to light, the buried metal laid upon the bank and refined from its dross out of the furnace, and then he thinks his pains well bestowed. And Henry turns it, as the poet means it to be turned, into a spur and a shame: “Go to the miners, thou sluggard in religion; consider their ways, and be wise.” Let their courage and diligence in seeking the wealth that perishes shame us out of our slothfulness in labouring for the true riches; for how much better is it to get wisdom than gold, and how much easier and safer — yet gold is sought for, and grace neglected. The witnesses do not divide; they let the mining hymn end at the very top of its power, with the hidden brought to light and the floods themselves bound at a word, so that the reader, dazzled by all a man can do, is exactly ripe for the question that all this splendour cannot answer.
12:
“But where shall wisdom be found? and where is the place of understanding?” — the refrain breaks in upon the glittering catalogue, and the witnesses hear it as the hinge of the whole chapter. The reformed John Gill draws the contrast the word “but” demands: though there is a vein for the silver and a place for the gold, and though brass and iron and bread-corn and brilliant gems are all wrung from the earth by the art and industry of men, so that their eyes behold every precious thing their minds desire, yet the question stands unanswered — what vein is there for wisdom, and where is the place in which it may be found? He takes it of the wisdom of God, which, though displayed in some measure in creation and providence, is nowhere fully searched out, least of all in his dealings with the children of men.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch mark that with this question the long description of mining attains the very end for which it was designed: man can find silver and gold by laying open the foundations of the earth, but wisdom he cannot so reach. They note that the word for wisdom carries the article, to give prominence to its transcendency over all the attainable things just named; and they distinguish the two terms of the verse, “understanding” being the faculty of seeing through what is distinguishable by the possession of right criteria, while “wisdom” is the perception of things in their true nature and their final causes. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott feels the sublime effect of the timing: with magnificent force this question comes in after the gigantic achievements of man just recounted, for notwithstanding all his industry, science, and skill, he is altogether ignorant of true wisdom; neither his knowledge nor his wealth can make him master of that, nor can he find it where he discovers so many other secret and precious things.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry names the jewel now sought — wisdom and understanding, the knowing and enjoying of God and ourselves — and will not grant that the men who found out all those ways to enrich themselves were therein truly wise; there is more real knowledge and happiness in sound divinity, which shows the way to heaven, than in all the natural philosophy that finds a way into the bowels of the earth. Two things, he says, cannot be found out concerning this wisdom, its price and its place, and the rest of the hymn will press each in turn. The wesleyan-arminian voices agree in raising it above every human science: Adam Clarke insists the terms are used in a sense wholly other than the arts and skills that fit a man for his animal and social state, and, reading the verse in the light of the chapter's close, finds wisdom to be true religion, another word for happiness, which comes only by Divine revelation; and John Wesley grants man one wisdom, to discover the works of nature and perform the operations of art, but the sublime wisdom that consists in the knowledge of God and ourselves no man can discover, save by the special gift of God.
13:
The first of the two things sought is the price, and the hymn declares it beyond all reckoning: “man knoweth not the price thereof; neither is it found in the land of the living.” The reformed John Gill takes the price two ways, of the worth men fail to set upon wisdom and of the equivalent none can find for it: were a man to offer all the substance of his house to learn the secret reasons of God's dealings, it would utterly be contemned, for no riches in the world can purchase such knowledge. He notes too the alternative rendering, “the order thereof,” the wise disposal of Providence and the reasons of it; and he spreads the saying over all its objects, over spiritual wisdom and grace, over the Gospel that carnal men reckon foolishness, and over Christ himself, chosen of God yet rejected and disallowed of men.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch guard the sense of the second clause, that wisdom is not found in “the land of the living” not as though it were absent from some bounded place, but that a man may search the whole world, and the subterranean deep, and the sea, and nowhere lay his hand upon it as upon a buried ore. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke lifts the verse into a great antithesis: wisdom is of infinite value, the only science that concerns both worlds, so that without it the wisest man is but a beast and with it the simplest is next to an angel; the world by its own wisdom never knew God, and true religion came by Divine revelation alone, while literature and science and art, for all their use, avail a man only for the present life.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry unfolds the price at length, and finds two faults in men. Few put a due value upon wisdom, knowing not its innate excellency nor their need of it, so that, though they have many a price in their hand, they have no heart to it, like the cock in the fable that would rather have lighted on a barley-corn than the jewel he found. And none can possibly give a valuable consideration for it, though he empty out the whole inventory of the world's treasures — gold named over and over, silver, and the precious stones — for it is a gift of the Holy Ghost that cannot be bought with money, as Peter told Simon in Acts 8:20; it does not run in the blood by descent, nor come by purchase, but is conferred without money and without price, because no money could be a price for it. Better, then, to get wisdom than gold, Henry concludes, for gold is another's and wisdom our own, gold for the body and time, wisdom for the soul and eternity. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the hymn has weighed wisdom against the whole wealth of the earth and found the scale unmoved.
14:
The hymn now sends its question ringing through the two great deeps and hears them answer: “the depth saith, It is not in me: and the sea saith, It is not with me.” The reformed John Gill makes the depth the deep places dug in the earth, the mines and their like, which, could they speak, would confess that they hold no metal or mineral, no ore or pearl or precious stone, of the value of wisdom or to be compared with it. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the two witnesses of the verse as the abyss and the sea, and take the point to be that wisdom lies nowhere directly present within a bounded space, at the bottom of no deep, nor to be had by any direct exchange: though a man search the land of the living, and the subterranean flood that feeds the visible waters, and the sea, the largest bounded expanse of that water, he shall not find it in any of them.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke turns the personification into a parable of the vanity of every earthly quest for happiness. Men may dig into the bowels of the earth and find gold and silver and gems, yet these will not give them true happiness; men may explore the foreign countries and, by navigation, knit together the most distant parts of the earth and multiply the comforts and luxuries of life, and yet every voyage and every enjoyment proclaims that true happiness is not here. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley keeps it briefer still: wisdom is not to be found in any part of the sea, though a man dig or dive ever so deep after it, nor to be learned from any creature. And the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, following the same two questions, bids us ask the miners, and by them the depth says it is not in me, and ask the mariners, and by them the sea says it is not with me; it can never be got by trading on the waters or diving into them, never sucked from the abundance of the seas or the treasures hidden in the sand. The witnesses do not divide; they gather round one confession, that the two most unfathomable regions men explore, the deep earth and the deep sea, for all that is drawn out of them return the same word — wisdom is not here. Where there is a vein for the silver there is no vein for wisdom; men break through greater difficulties to reach the wealth of this world than the wisdom of the next, and take more pains to learn how to live in this world than how to live for ever in a better.
15:
Having declared that wisdom is nowhere to be found, the hymn now shows that it is nowhere to be bought, and the witnesses watch Job descend to particulars: “it cannot be gotten for gold, neither shall silver be weighed for the price thereof.” The reformed John Gill notes that Job instances first in gold as the most valuable of metals, and fastens on the very word used for it, which signifies “shut up” — gold being first shut up in the earth out of which it is dug, and then shut up again among the treasures of men — so that the line runs, more literally, “gold shall not be given instead of it” as a sufficient price or valuable consideration.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke drives the point home with the great example of a king who had all that gold could buy: genuine religion and true happiness are not to be acquired by earthly property, and though Solomon made gold and silver as plentiful as the stones of Jerusalem and had every delight of the sons of men, yet he was not happy; he had wisdom, being the wisest of men, but not the wisdom of which Job here speaks, and therefore to him all was vanity and vexation of spirit — sentiments, Clarke adds, exactly such as we might expect if Solomon were indeed, as some suppose, the author of the book.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, drawing up his inventory of the world's most valuable treasures, marvels that gold is named over and over and silver besides, with the precious stones to follow, and yet not all of them heaped together, no, nor all the substance of a man's house, could be a valuable consideration for wisdom; these may give a man some advantage in the seeking, as they did to Solomon, but there is no purchasing wisdom with them, for it is the gift of the Holy Ghost and comes without money and without price. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the couplet to the same effect, that pure gold cannot be given for wisdom and silver cannot be weighed out as its price, and carry the thought straight on into the catalogue of gems that follows, where fine gold of Ophir and the costliest stones will be arraigned one by one and found wanting. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the poet, having emptied the deep and the sea of wisdom, now empties the treasury too, laying the purest gold and the weighed silver on the counter and finding that the one thing worth having is precisely the one thing that money cannot reach.
16:
The reckoning of the price now opens the jewel-casket, and the witnesses turn appraisers: “it cannot be valued with the gold of Ophir, with the precious onyx, or the sapphire.” The reformed John Gill takes the gold of Ophir for the choicest gold of all, and the onyx and sapphire for two of the stones that shone in the high priest's breastplate; Pliny, he recalls, places the onyx in Arabia, near which Job lived and with whose worth he must have been well acquainted, and yet none of these, gold or gem, is of the value of wisdom or sufficient to purchase it. He notes that the word rendered “valued” may also be read “strowed,” as goods are spread out when set to sale, so that wisdom is not so much as to be laid on the same counter with these.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke pauses here to lay out the whole treasury named in these verses, the several words for gold and the seven kinds of precious stone, and on one point his mineralogy carries a real correction. The stone the Hebrew calls sappir, he argues, is not our modern sapphire at all: when its description in Scripture is set beside Pliny's account of a stone that glitters with golden points and is nowhere transparent, it must be an opaque, spotted stone, and Clarke conjectures the lapis lazuli, blue with golden-like specks formed by pyrites of iron, the very stone from which the unfading ultramarine is ground. The onyx he makes a species of chalcedony, named from its likeness to a man's nail; and so, gem by gem, he shows how uncertain the old names are and how easily the costliest stone may be mistaken — a fit under-song to a passage whose whole burden is that these dazzling things, however named, cannot be weighed against wisdom. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the line that wisdom is not outweighed with the fine gold of Ophir, nor with the precious onyx and the sapphire, and set it among the couplets that pile jewel upon jewel only to abase them all. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the hymn, in naming Ophir's gold and the breastplate stones, chooses the very highest tokens of earthly worth on purpose, so that the reader who follows the appraisal down its glittering list may feel with what an infinite margin wisdom overtops them.
17:
The appraisal continues, and the witnesses weigh two more of the shining things against wisdom: “the gold and the crystal cannot equal it: and the exchange of it shall not be for jewels of fine gold.” The reformed John Gill lingers over the crystal, which he takes to have been far more prized of old than now, found in certain islands of the Red Sea that Job might well have known, one of them bearing, from the very stone gathered there, the name Topazion; he recalls from Pliny a crystal vessel sold for a sum answering to more than a thousand pounds, and the two crystal cups that Nero, hearing of his losses, broke in his fury, that no other man might drink from them. Some, Gill allows, render the word “amber,” a thing far-fetched and therefore costly, and Pliny ranks it with the gems; while the ancient versions read “glass,” whose first making, he notes, was near Judea, at the roots of Mount Carmel by the river Belus, and at Sidon in Phoenicia, a city famed of old for the working of it — so that whether crystal, amber, or glass be meant, the point holds, that none of them can equal wisdom.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the pair “gold and glass are not equal to it, nor is it exchanged for jewels of gold,” and settle on glass for the transparent thing here named, observing that the ancient tongues had common names for glass and that this rare and precious manufacture was fitly ranked among treasures. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott offers the alternative that the closing word may mean not “the exchange” but “the attraction” of wisdom; and then, feeling that the sustained sublimity of the passage needs no gloss, he declares that the remainder of the chapter calls for little remark, its unrivalled grandeur being patent and comment superfluous. He notes only the broad likeness between this chapter and the great chapter on wisdom in Proverbs 8, both of them seeming to imply a knowledge of the Mosaic narrative of creation. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that whether the transparent treasure be crystal or glass, and whether the last word speak of bartering wisdom or of being drawn toward it, the verse does its office in the mounting inventory, adding the clearest and costliest of wrought things to the heap that the hymn has resolved to set at nothing beside the one pearl it is seeking.
18:
The catalogue nears its end, and the witnesses take up the sea's own jewels: “no mention shall be made of coral, or of pearls: for the price of wisdom is above rubies.” The reformed John Gill identifies the coral as the marine growth, hard as stone yet reckoned among precious things, of which a place on the Red Sea shore, Coralia, may have taken its name; the pearls he draws from the shellfish of the sea. But he owns that the two Hebrew words behind “coral” and “pearls” are of uncertain sense, left untranslated by some and taken by others for precious stones unknown, so named because found in high places; the Targum renders the first by a word for the sardonyx, and other scholars by yet other stones, so that here, as so often in this passage, the exact gem cannot be fixed with certainty.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the couplet that pearls and crystal are not to be mentioned and that the getting of wisdom is beyond corals, ranking these among the costly things, the chapatzim, that the wisdom-writings elsewhere set below her. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, still unfolding his catalogue of the seven stones, dwells on the last-named of them and raises a genuine question of identity. The coral, in his mineralogy, grows head downwards from the marine rocky caverns of the Mediterranean, and the pearls are formed coat upon coat within the shellfish of the eastern seas; but it is over the last-named stone that his real question falls. The word our translators render “rubies,” he says, is peninim, which many take for the ruby, the blood-red six-sided stone; but some learned men judge it rather the loadstone, the magnet, so named from its turning to the north, and Clarke half inclines to them, for the clause would then read that the “attraction” of wisdom is beyond that of the peninim — gold and gems and the very loadstone drawing the heart of man strongly, yet wisdom, when it is understood, drawing more strongly than all, since the loadstone can attract but iron, while wisdom draws a man clean away from all earthly entanglements to seek and to intermeddle with all understanding. The witnesses do not divide over the burden of the verse; they part only over the naming of its stones, whether coral or sardonyx, whether ruby or loadstone, and agree that the poet, sweeping in the treasures of the sea to join those of the mine, still finds the whole hoard light in the balance, for the price of wisdom is above them all.
19:
The last of the jewels is brought and weighed, and the appraisal closes: “the topaz of Ethiopia shall not equal it, neither shall it be valued with pure gold.” The reformed John Gill is careful about the country named, which he takes to be not the Abyssinian Ethiopia beyond Egypt, where, he says, gems are rare or wanting, but the land of Cush, the Arabia adjoining Midian, near Job's own country — the same region whose daughter Zipporah is called an Ethiopian woman. There, he shows from the old geographers, the topaz was in fact found: Diodorus Siculus tells of an island in the Arabian gulf, held by the Troglodytes, where the topaz is gathered, a clear stone like glass yet shining with a wonderful golden colour; and Strabo, that this same isle was cleared of the serpents that killed the men who came for the topaz, and that the stone is so refulgent it can hardly be seen by day for the light around it, but is marked at night by its shining and dug out in the dark.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke agrees that the Cush here meant is the Ethiopia stretching from the eastern coast of the Red Sea toward Lower Egypt, and repeats from Diodorus the account of the topaz found in abundance on the isle of serpents; yet he cannot vouch for its correctness, judging the tale to have too much of the legend in it, and leaves the reader to consult the place. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the verse that the topaz of Ethiopia is not equal to wisdom and that she is not outweighed by pure fine gold, closing the long inventory of couplets with the same verdict that opened it. The witnesses do not divide; they let the appraisal end where it must, the golden topaz of a far and famous coast laid in the scale beside the purest refined gold, and both together lifted like a feather against the weight of wisdom. So the whole treasury of earth and sea has now been told over — silver and gold, onyx and sapphire, crystal, coral, pearls, rubies, and topaz — and every last precious thing has been set down and found insufficient; the price of wisdom has been asked of all the world's wealth, and the world's wealth has fallen dumb. Not one stone of all the priest's breastplate, not one metal of all the miner's hoard, has been able to name a price; and with the whole treasury thus silenced, the poet stands free to raise his question a second time, and to seek its answer where alone, the witnesses agree, it was ever to be had.
20:
“Whence then cometh wisdom? and where is the place of understanding?” — the refrain returns unchanged, and the witnesses treat its repetition as no idle echo. The reformed John Gill says the same questions are put again to set forth the surpassing excellency of wisdom and to carry the discourse forward to what is yet to be said of it. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke notes only that the words are nearly the same as at the first asking, and John Wesley, hearing the second cry, finds in it the turn of the whole hymn: by this diligent inquiry we come at length to see that there is a twofold wisdom, one hid in God, which belongs not to us, and the other revealed to man, which belongs to us and to our children.

It is the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry who dwells longest on the repeated question, and reads it as a matter too weighty to be let fall until the enquiry speed. The knowledge of God's secret will, he says — the reasons of what he is doing now and the particulars of what he will do hereafter — is out of our reach, high, and we cannot attain unto it; it is hid from the eyes of all the living, and the line and plummet of human reason can never fathom the abyss of the divine counsels. Job and his friends had been disputing about the methods and reasons of Providence, and “what fools are we,” Henry has Job say, “to fight in the dark thus, to dispute about that which we do not understand.” Let us be content, then, not to know the future events of Providence until time discover them, as the risen Lord told the disciples in Acts 1:7, and not to know its secret reasons until eternity discover them; for God is now a God that hideth himself, as Isaiah 45:15 confesses, with clouds and darkness round about him.

Yet Henry will not leave the question in despair, for the verses that follow it answer it in two stages: this wisdom, though hidden from us, is not hidden from God, in whom it is treasured as the apostle says in Ephesians 3:9, and there is besides a second wisdom, plain and within our reach, which the close of the hymn will name. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the refrain is repeated because it must be pressed until it is answered, and that the answer will come not by any deeper mining of the earth or the sea but by lifting the whole search up out of the creature and into the Creator, from whom alone both the wisdom that is hid and the wisdom that is given proceed.
21:
The answer to the twice-asked question begins by shutting every door in creation: “seeing it is hid from the eyes of all living, and kept close from the fowls of the air.” The latin-fathers Gregory the Great takes the veiling as a lesson in holy self-abasement: what wonder is it, he asks, if the Eternal Wisdom of God cannot be seen, when the very invisible created things cannot be embraced by the eyes of men? By the things that are made we learn with what lowliness to revere the Creator of all, so that in this life the human mind should not dare to usurp to itself anything of that Appearance of the Almighty which he reserves for his Elect as their reward in the recompense to come. And on the second clause, that wisdom is kept close from the fowls of the air, Gregory draws his accustomed distinction, that birds in Scripture are taken now in a good sense and now in a bad — sometimes the very powers of the air, the evil spirits that beset the minds of men and, like the fowls that devoured the seed by the wayside, pluck the word of life out of the memory.

The reformed John Gill will not let “all living” be lowered to the beasts of the field, which would make the sentiment jejune, but takes it of rational creatures, of men: the wisdom of God, though displayed in his works, is but imperfectly known by them, and the secret reasons of his providential dealings are hid from all at present, as is his spiritual wisdom, and the Gospel of Christ, and Christ himself, hidden from the eyes of the most prudent natural men. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry presses the wonder of the fowls: this wisdom is hid from the eyes of all the living, of philosophers and politicians and saints alike, and kept close even from the birds of heaven, which fly high and, as an earlier chapter says of the eagle in ch. 39:29, behold afar off; yet though man is wiser than the fowls of heaven, and though those who soar highest in their speculations think themselves above the heads of other men, none of them can penetrate the counsels of God. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley gathers it into a rule of patience: the line and plummet of human reason can never sound the abyss of the divine counsels, and we must be content not to know the future events of Providence till time reveal them, nor its secret reasons till eternity bring them to light. The witnesses do not divide; from the church father to the moderns they agree that wisdom is hid from the sharpest eye that lives and the highest wing that flies, so that the search must turn from every creature to God alone.
22:
“Destruction and death say, We have heard the fame thereof with our ears” — the hymn calls up the last and darkest witnesses, and they too can give but a rumour. The reformed John Gill takes destruction and death for the region of the dead, the pit and the grave, and hears in the verse the voice of those who, while they lived, had only a report of this wisdom; question their records and traditions, and the sum of what they can tell amounts to no more than a distant fame. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the line that destruction and death say, with our ears we heard a report of it, and set the verse against the foregoing: no living creature could answer the question, and even the birds that fly aloft could give no tidings, and now the realm of Abaddon and of death below has heard, at most, but the echo of wisdom's name.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fastens on the first word, Abaddon, the destroyer, and his offspring death, and observes that this is the very name given to the great enemy in Revelation 9:11, Abaddon, rendered in the Greek Apollyon; no wonder, he says, that death and the destroyer have only heard the fame of wisdom and no more, seeing that the close of the chapter defines it as the fear of the Lord and a departure from evil, things point-blank contrary to the interest of Satan and the enlargement of the empire of death. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads the same fitness the other way: that destruction and death should have heard the fame of wisdom is natural enough, since wisdom consists in departing from the very evil that leads men down to their abode. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley hears in the verse a gleam of hope beyond the grave: though these dark regions cannot give an account of wisdom themselves, there is a world upon which they border where it shall be seen clearly, and Death seems to say, Have patience, I will fetch thee shortly to a place where even this wisdom shall be found; when the veil of flesh is rent and the interposing clouds are scattered, we shall know what God does, though we know it not now. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the poet has now questioned the whole compass of being, the living and the dead, the heights and the depths, and every last quarter has returned the same answer — that wisdom is not theirs to give, but at the utmost a name they have heard.
23:
“God understandeth the way thereof, and he knoweth the place thereof” — at last the hymn names the one who holds the secret, and the witnesses rest upon it as the turn of the whole. The reformed John Gill takes the words to mean God, and God only: not the way by which men might come at wisdom, which is still past finding out, but the way that wisdom itself takes, deep and untraceable, and the very grounds and reasons of the course it keeps, which none but the Lord understands. He carries the confession, after his manner, to Christ, the wisdom of God, whose way in the eternal council and covenant of grace, and in the fulness of time in the assuming of human nature, God alone comprehends.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke draws the practical conclusion, that wisdom can be taught only by a revelation from God himself; and he adds a small matter of the text, that where the received reading has “understandeth,” six manuscripts and the Septuagint read a kindred word meaning “hath established” or “disposed” her way — God hath well ordered the way of wisdom — a variant that touches the wording without altering the sense that God alone commands it. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott makes the verse the seat of a deeper reflection: God is the author of wisdom and his fear the beginning of it, so that with his infinite knowledge of the universe he cannot but be cognisant of its way and place. He observes that while the foundation of wisdom is coeval with that of the world, the very existence of wisdom in relation to man implies the existence of evil, for except by departing from evil there could for man be no wisdom — wrong itself being but what is wrung aside from the right. And he lifts the thought toward the Gospel, that wisdom, or that which ranks with it, is after all to be purchased by the poor, as the prophet cries in Isaiah 55:1, and as Christ made the kingdom a pearl of great price yet preached it above all to the poor. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley keeps the sense close and plain: God alone knows the way, the methods he takes in the management of all affairs with their grounds and ends, and the place, where wisdom dwells, which is only in his own mind. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the long quest is answered not by a discovery but by a Person, and that the wisdom no creature could find is understood perfectly by the God who made both the world and the search.
24:
The hymn now grounds God's knowledge of wisdom in his boundless survey of all things: “for he looketh to the ends of the earth, and seeth under the whole heaven.” The reformed John Gill reads the verse as the reason that must make God the sole knower of wisdom's way and place: since all the parts and quarters of the earth, even to its utmost ends, lie open to his sight, and nothing in heaven or earth or hell is hidden from him, there can be no way of wisdom nor place for it that he does not see, wherever it directs its course or takes up its abode. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke compresses the whole into a sentence, that God's knowledge is unlimited and his power infinite; and John Wesley enlarges the same thought, that he and he only knows wisdom because his providence is infinite and universal, reaching to all places and all times, past and present and to come, whereas the most knowing of men have but narrow understandings, and the wisdom and justice and beauty of God's works are not fully seen until all their parts are laid together.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry unfolds the verse as the first of two proofs that God alone understands his own way. He that governs the world is omniscient, for he looks to the ends of the earth, both in place and in time; distant ages and distant regions are alike under his view, while we are short-sighted and know little of what is doing in the world, much less of what shall be done. The eyes of the Lord are in every place, nay, they run to and fro through the whole earth, and nothing is or can be hidden from him; and therefore the reasons why some wicked men prosper remarkably and others are as remarkably punished, secret as they are to us, are known to him. One day's events and one man's affairs have such reference to and dependence on another's that only he to whom all events and all affairs are naked and open, and who sees the whole at one entire and certain view, is a competent judge of every part. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the hymn answers its own great question by lifting the eye from the miner's lamp, which lights a single shaft, to the all-seeing gaze that takes in the ends of the earth at once — and that a God who sees so must needs know where wisdom dwells, for nothing whatever escapes him.
25:
The proof of God's all-governing exactness is drawn from the lightest and most fluid of things: “to make the weight for the winds; and he weigheth the waters by measure.” The reformed John Gill dwells on the winds first: God makes the wind itself, holds it in his fists and brings it out of his treasures, gives it its bent toward this or that point of the heavens and the force it shall blow with, greater or lesser, for men's good or their chastening; he raises the stormy wind and makes it subside into a calm, and can add to or take from its weight so that it presses more or less upon the bodies it meets. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the “weight for the winds” as the very gravity of the atmosphere, so nicely proportioned to the needs of all that lives that by it the blood circulates in the veins and the sap in the plants, and respiration itself is possible; and “he weigheth the waters by measure” he takes of the exact proportion God has set between the waters and the dry land, the aqueous surface being to the earth as three to one, that there might be evaporation enough to store the air with moisture for the watering of the ground.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws the argument the verse is built for: God manages the winds by weight, appointing to every wind that blows its season and proportion and bounds, when and where and how much and how long it shall blow; and he instances these lightest and least certain of things on purpose, that we may the more strongly infer he does the same in weightier matters, ordering all things in the most exact weight and measure. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry marvels at the same paradox, that what is lighter than the wind should yet be poised and weighed: God makes the weight for the winds, bringing them out of his treasuries, as the psalmist sings in Psalm 135:7, and keeping an exact account of what he draws out, not scattering them at random; and the waters of the sea and the rain he both weighs and measures, allotting the proportion of every tide and every shower. If Providence be thus exact, Henry reasons, in the wind and the rain, how much more in dispensing frowns and favours to the children of men according to the rules of equity. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the God who has fixed a weight for the very winds must order all things by wisdom, and that the hymn is teaching us to read his hidden justice off the visible precision of his world.
26:
The catalogue of God's ordering laws goes on, reaching to the storm: “when he made a decree for the rain, and a way for the lightning of the thunder.” The reformed John Gill takes the decree for the rain to mean that God appointed within himself to give it — rain being his gift alone, which none of the vanities of the heathen can bestow, a blessing he sends upon good and bad, now on one place and now on another, in greater or lesser showers, and withholds again at his sovereign pleasure. The thunder he owns for the voice of God, the word standing in the plural for its many claps, and the lightning as that which commonly goes with it, seen before it is heard because the eye is quicker than the ear; and he notes Broughton's rendering, that God made a bound for the rain and a way for the lightning and the thunder together.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke turns the decree into the very process of the rain: God determined how it should be generated, the sun's heat drawing up the vapours, which, lighter than the air, ascend until they reach a region of their own density, are gathered into clouds, and, when driven together and condensed by the winds or by the passage of the lightning, fall again as rain, in drops greater or smaller according to the force that drove them. The “way for the lightning of the thunder” he reads with care, the word for lightning coming from a root that means to notch or indent, so that it names exactly the zigzag form the flash takes in passing from cloud to cloud — a thing, he says, he has watched for hours together. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the verse and carry it straight into the two that follow, when God appointed to the rain its law and the course to the lightning of the thunder, then he saw wisdom and declared it. And the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley refers it all to the first creation, when God settled the course that should thenceforth be continued, the decree being an appointment, a standing statute-law, that the rain should fall in such times and places and proportions. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the poet is numbering the fixed laws by which God rules the sky — the measured rain, the appointed path of the lightning — as further evidence that the world is governed by an ordering wisdom, and that at the founding of these laws wisdom stood already, seen and known, in the mind of God.
27:
The founding of the world's laws is joined, in this verse, to God's perfect possession of wisdom in the act: “then did he see it, and declare it; he prepared it, yea, and searched it out.” The reformed John Gill takes the “it” for God's own wisdom, which, when he made and executed his decrees for the rain and the lightning and the thunder, he saw in himself and saw again as it appeared in his works, looking upon all and approving it as very good, and then declared it to others by those very works of nature and providence that everywhere publish it. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the four verbs as the stages of a finished work: when God had completed his creative operations and tried and proved them, investigating and finding them very good, then he gave to man the needful revelation — the fear of the Lord that the next verse will name.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott finds the very choice of terms remarkable, and draws out their force: God's dealing with wisdom is described as seeing, which is intuition; as declaring or numbering, which is ratiocination; as preparing or establishing, which is determination; and as searching out, which is investigation — and each of these implies the operation of mind, and so stands opposed to the fatality of an impersonal law or the fixed necessity of a blind nature. Keil and Delitzsch, the other grammatical-historical voice, render the line to the same effect, that God then saw wisdom and declared it, took it as a pattern and tested it also, at the very moment of appointing the rain its law. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley guards the words from misuse: God saw wisdom within himself, looking upon it in his own mind as the rule by which he would proceed in the creation and government of all things, and prepared it as if he had long been making ready his materials, and searched it out — not that searching implies in him any ignorance or need of time and industry, which were repugnant to his perfections, but that he did all things with an absolute and perfect wisdom, as exactly as if he had spent long study to find them out. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry notes that some read the verse of wisdom as a person, “then he saw her and showed her,” and so hear in it an anticipation of that essential Wisdom of the Father, the eternal Word who was by him before ever the earth was, of whom Solomon speaks in Proverbs 8:22 and John at the opening of his Gospel. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that at the laying of the world's foundations wisdom was already God's own, seen and declared and prepared and proved by him — and if it was so wholly his in the making of all things, then his it remains to give.
28:
“And unto man he said, Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom; and to depart from evil is understanding” — the whole long ascent comes to rest on this single word, and the witnesses gather about it as the crown of the hymn. The reformed John Gill turns first to the question, to whom the word was spoken. Some render it “unto Adam,” taking it of the first man, whether by the law written on his heart or by the express command not to eat of the tree of knowledge, obedience to which would have been his highest wisdom; but Gill judges it best understood in general of the sons of men, the substance of all that God says in his works and in his word, whereby it appears that the whole of man is to fear God and keep his commandments.

The wesleyan-arminian voices press the reference to Adam and draw out the remedy the verse prescribes. Adam Clarke reads it as the revelation God gave the first man after his fall, who had sought wisdom in a forbidden way, seeing the tree pleasant to make one wise, as Genesis 3:6 tells, and so lost the wisdom he had and became foolish and miserable; the cure is to fear the Lord and set him always before the eyes, and to depart from the evil within and the evil without. John Wesley takes it of God's word spoken to Adam in the day he was created and, in him, to all his posterity, first written on the mind with God's own finger and afterward taught by patriarchs and prophets; the “Behold” marks at once the great importance of the doctrine and man's backwardness to receive it, and the whole names true religion in its two branches, the fear of the Lord which is doing good, and the departing from evil which is forsaking sin. And Wesley finds in the close Job's own vindication, that he had ever esteemed it his best wisdom to fear God and depart from evil, and so was no hypocrite as his friends had charged.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott will not have the verse read as a bare historical statement, yet holds it profoundly and universally true, that it is the wisdom of man as man to fear the Lord and depart from evil, and that this is God's primary revelation, underlying all others; and he marks a delicate point of the text, that the name here rendered “the Lord” is not the four-lettered name Jehovah which Job used in ch. 12:9, but the other divine name, later everywhere put by the Jews in its room. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the doctrine of it all: the fear of the Lord is the spring and summary of all religion, a filial fear springing from high thoughts of God, and it appears by a constant care to depart from evil, so that the verse agrees exactly with God's own character of Job at ch. 1:1. The witnesses do not finally divide, though Gill would spread the word over all mankind and Clarke and Wesley fix it first on Adam; they agree that the hymn, having ransacked the mine and the sea and the grave for a wisdom no creature could yield, comes home at last to a wisdom God has plainly given — not to fathom his secret counsels, but to fear him and forsake evil — and that here, and here alone, the searching soul is told where its true wisdom lies.
